Women walk at a platform during peak hours at Churchgate station in Mumbai, India [File: Rajanish Kakade/AP]By Priyanka ShankarPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
India lifted nearly 500 million out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent in the world’s most populous nation during the same period, according to a new report by the World Bank.
The only other parallel in poverty reduction on this scale is China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty — though that was over a period of 40 years.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest companylist 2 of 3India’s largest dam planned to counter China faces Indigenous revoltlist 3 of 3India protesters march with 1km banner of deleted voters’ namesend of list
Yet despite the substantial fall in poverty in India — home to 1.4 billion people — the income and wealth inequality gap has widened significantly since it opened up its economy in the early 1990s.
According to the 2026 World Inequality Report, inequality in India remains among the highest in the world.
We take a look at how India managed to almost eradicate extreme poverty, and at the contrast between that accomplishment and the deep economic inequality that remains in the world’s most populous nation:
What does the World Bank data say?
Based on an extreme poverty threshold of $3 a day, the World Bank said extreme poverty in India declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023.
Extreme poverty is defined as the minimum amount of money needed to afford basic essentials such as food, water, shelter and clothing.

US Midterms 2026: The country is about to get a new Congress. What do voters want? | This Is AmericaBy Evan SemonesPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Polls have opened in some parts of the United States for Tuesday’s pivotal midterm elections, with all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats being contested.
Voting hours are determined and set by each state. The first polls have opened in Vermont, New Jersey, Virginia, Connecticut and Kentucky, with other states set to start election day voting soon.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Supreme Court rejects Trump request to set aside California ballotslist 2 of 3US midterms 2026: What polls reveal about Democratic, Republican voterslist 3 of 3Trump approval rating near record low on eve of US midterm elections: Pollend of list
More than 57 million Americans have already cast early ballots, with some of the heaviest voting coming from some of this year’s biggest political battlegrounds: Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
Voters in 36 states will also elect governors.
Republicans currently have a majority (53) in the 100-seat Senate. Democrats and independents who caucus with the party hold 47. Republicans also have a narrow four-seat majority in the House.
Democrats have campaigned on promises to address the nation’s cost-of-living crisis and end Trump’s war on Iran.
They are eyeing historic gains in both houses of Congress that could ultimately change the trajectory of the US president’s final two years in office.
Republicans, however, are hoping to defy political gravity.

Fishing boats sit idle in the Strait of Hormuz, near Qeshm Island, Iran [File: Majid Saeedi/Getty Images]By Edna Mohamed and ReutersPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Amid growing concerns about renewed attacks on Iran following Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, US forces have struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what officials have reportedly described as a defensive measure.
In the first attack since June on Qeshm Island, which serves as the primary platform for Iran’s “asymmetric” naval power, according to analysts, the US strikes come as both sides continue to adopt military and diplomatic postures.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How will the Iran war shape the outcome of the US midterm vote?list 2 of 3How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surgelist 3 of 3China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetingsend of list
Mediation efforts led by Qatar are continuing in a bid to avert a return to all-out war, which began on February 28 when the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran, triggering the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz, surging oil and gas prices and massive damage to military, civil and energy facilities around the Gulf.
Here’s what we know:
What happened in the attack on Qeshm Island?
Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island late on Monday, as US media reported that the US military had carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.
The blasts came in rapid succession, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast along the waterway.

Rubble left after fires at Alneam market after a drone attack in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan, October 20, 2026 [Handout via Reuters]By Mohammad MansourPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
The Sudanese government’s allegations that Ethiopia is behind a deadly wave of unmanned aerial assaults belie a deep and longstanding rift between the two countries, which threatens to intensify internal conflicts in both.
Sudan has officially lodged complaints with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over allegations that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary – which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since April 2023 – is using Ethiopian territory to launch attacks against civilian sites, including power stations.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of faminelist 2 of 3Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spreelist 3 of 3Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power systemend of list
Ethiopia’s alleged support for the RSF has triggered differences within the SAF on how to respond next, Sudanese border affairs specialist Abdul Kareem Al-Almin Ahmed told Al Jazeera.
“The mutual accusations are many and almost daily, and the tension on the part of the Sudanese army has reached high levels, to the degree that made some voices inside the Sudanese army and the forces allied with it demand that Sudan declare war on Ethiopia based on these interventions,” Al-Almin told Al Jazeera.

Russia has bombed a hospital in Kharkiv, injuring at least 73 people, while also carrying out several attacks on energy infrastructure across multiple Ukrainian regions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X that “the Russians directly struck a city clinical hospital. Seventy-three people were injured, and the cardiology department, where people were receiving treatment, was damaged.”

Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov confirmed on Telegram that the hospital sustained heavy damage in Monday night’s bombardment, with more than 1,000 windows shattered.
Separately, Ukrainian energy sites were hit, including in Kharkiv, in what President Zelenskyy described as a “complex, massive attack”.
“The main target was energy – power generation facilities and substations – in the Odesa, Cherkasy, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Chernivtsi, Chernihiv, and Rivne regions,” he said in a post on X.
Zelenskyy added that Russia had launched 289 attack drones overnight, as well as 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles. This comes a day after at least 31 people were killed in a Russian strike on an aid distribution centre.

Electricity cables attached to utility poles in Beirut, Lebanon [File: Mohamed Azakir/Reuters]By Justin SalhaniPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Beirut, Lebanon – Lebanon’s Ministry of Energy and Water has begun shutting down the supply of electricity to approximately 100 public institutions that have outstanding bill payments, according to local media.
The decision, which began to take effect on Monday, marks a further escalation in Energy Minister Joe Saddi’s dispute with the government. Saddi recently began boycotting cabinet meetings over what he claims is the government’s failure to address his demands to increase power supply, reduce the burden of fuel costs and settle unpaid bills to the state-owned electricity company.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of warlist 2 of 3Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we knowlist 3 of 3Israel’s war on homesend of list
Lebanon has struggled with power cuts for years, but state-provided electricity dropped sharply following the 2019 economic and banking crisis. In Beirut, for example, electricity supplied by the state was once available for about 21 hours a day, but that has dropped in recent years to just two to four hours, with some days seeing no power at all.
Analysts say that deep structural issues are behind the Lebanese state’s failure to provide electricity in recent years and without deep reform, little is likely to change.
“The key problem in the power sector is, as everyone knows, that we have a lot of corruption,” said Jessica Obeid, a Lebanese energy expert. “This sector has corruption across the entire supply chain, and it’s in the billions of dollars, so it is not something that is going to disappear overn...
